The Po River. Northern Italy's longest river, flowing four hundred and five miles from the Alps westward across the Padana plain to the Adriatic Sea. It created Italy's most fertile agricultural region and enabled the rise of medieval city-states like Venice and Milan.

The Po originates in the Maritime Alps and flows eastward across the Padana, or Po Valley, Italy's most productive agricultural and industrial region. The Po delta near Venice is a complex network of lagoons, marshes, and waterways. Venice's foundation depended entirely on Po-valley grain supplies. Medieval northern Italian city-states like Milan, Padua, and Ferrara grew wealthy controlling sections of the Po and its tributaries.

The river is historically prone to catastrophic flooding. The nineteen fifty-one flood devastated northern Italy and prompted modern flood-control infrastructure. Today the Po is subject to heavy pollution from industrial and agricultural runoff. Modern water quality in the lower Po is a major environmental concern. The Po valley remains Italy's breadbasket. Wheat, rice, corn, and other crops flourish in its alluvial soils.

The Po is the defining river of northern Italy's geography and history. Venice's food supply, trade, and political power depended entirely on Po-valley territories. Milan, a major inland city, had power that relied on Po commerce and tributaries. Padua was a medieval university city built on a Po tributary. Many Renaissance city-states that shaped European culture and learning were Po-valley powers, and the river provided the foundation for their wealth and influence.
